TASK ID: three-coloring-to-one-in-three-sat

USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from 3-Coloring to 1-in-3-SAT. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is 3-Coloring and TARGET is 1-in-3-SAT. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = ThreeColoring
3-Coloring (graph 3-colorability).

Instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...]}
  * Vertices are 0..n-1. Edges are undirected pairs [u, v] with u != v;
    [u, v] and [v, u] are the same edge and may not both appear.

Yes iff each vertex can be given one of 3 colours so that the two
endpoints of every edge get different colours. Not every colour has to
be used.

Edge cases: n = 0 is yes. Any graph with at most 3 vertices is yes. A
graph containing 4 mutually adjacent vertices (K4) is no.

TARGET = OneInThreeSat
1-in-3-SAT (positive one-in-three satisfiability).

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[a, b, c], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m.
  * Every clause lists exactly 3 different variables, all as positive
    integers: negated literals are not allowed in this problem.
  * Variable order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes EXACTLY ONE
of the three variables in every clause true.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is yes, for any m, including
m = 0. A formula with clauses needs m >= 3.

INPUT FILES: ["problems.py"]
WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-l_ij7dq3
All input files are in this directory; run every command from it and write your files here. problems.py is long (about 500 lines): you do not need to read it to know the formats, which are given above. It provides SOURCE and TARGET with is_yes(instance), validate(instance) and random_instance(rng, scale); search it (e.g. with grep) only if you need something specific.

REQUIRED OUTPUT: create reduce.py in the workspace, defining
    reduce(instance) -> instance
It takes an instance of the source problem and returns an instance of the target problem, both in the formats documented in problems.py. The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

You may read files such as problems.py, but do not run, execute or test any code. Write reduce.py, then submit.
Do not merely describe code: leave the files at those exact paths.

def validate_cnf(clauses: Any, num_vars: Any) -> None:
    """Check a DIMACS-style clause list over variables 1..num_vars."""
    require_int(num_vars, "num_vars", minimum=0)
    require(isinstance(clauses, list), "clauses must be a list")
    for clause in clauses:
        require(isinstance(clause, list), f"each clause must be a list, got {clause!r}")
        for literal in clause:
            require(is_int(literal), f"literals must be ints, got {literal!r}")
            require(
                literal != 0 and abs(literal) <= num_vars,
                f"literal {literal} is outside ±1..±{num_vars}",
            )


# --- Shared generation helpers ---------------------------------------------


def all_graphs(n: int) -> Iterator[list[list[int]]]:
    """Every labelled simple graph on n vertices, as an edge list.
    There are 2^(n(n-1)/2) of them: 1,024 at n = 5, 32,768 at n = 6."""
    pairs = list(combinations(range(n), 2))
    for mask in range(1 << len(pairs)):
        yield [list(pair) for index, pair in enumerate(pairs) if mask >> index & 1]


def random_graph(rng: random.Random, n: int, p: float | None = None) -> list[list[int]]:
    """Edge list with each edge present with probability p (random if None)."""
    p = rng.random() if p is None else p
    return [[u, v] for u, v in combinations(range(n), 2) if rng.random() < p]

"""Polynomial-time reduction from 3-Coloring to positive 1-in-3-SAT.

Source instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...]}
Target instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[a, b, c], ...]}

Construction
------------
For every vertex v (0 <= v < n) and colour c in {1, 2, 3} introduce a Boolean
variable x(v, c), meaning "vertex v receives colour c".

  * Clause [x(v,1), x(v,2), x(v,3)] for every vertex v.  A 1-in-3 clause is
    satisfied exactly when one of its variables is true, so this forces each
    vertex to receive exactly one colour.

  * For every edge {u, v} and every colour c, introduce a fresh auxiliary
    variable y(u,v,c) and the clause [x(u,c), x(v,c), y(u,v,c)].  This clause
    is unsatisfiable iff both x(u,c) and x(v,c) are true; otherwise the
    auxiliary variable can be set to make it satisfied.  Hence it forbids the
    two endpoints of an edge from sharing colour c.  Each auxiliary occurs in
    exactly one clause, so distinct edge constraints never interfere.

The formula is satisfiable iff the graph has a proper 3-colouring.

Size: 3*n + 3*|E| variables and n + 3*|E| clauses, so the reduction runs in
polynomial time.
"""


def reduce(instance):
    n = instance["n"]
    edges = instance["edges"]

    # x(v, c) for v in 0..n-1, c in 1..3, numbered 1..3n.
    def x(v, c):
        return 3 * v + c

    clauses = []

    # Exactly one colour per vertex.
    for v in range(n):
        clauses.append([x(v, 1), x(v, 2), x(v, 3)])

    # Forbid equal colours on the endpoints of every edge.
    next_var = 3 * n
    for u, v in edges:
        for c in (1, 2, 3):
            next_var += 1
            y = next_var
            clauses.append([x(u, c), x(v, c), y])

    return {"num_vars": next_var, "clauses": clauses}

"""Polynomial-time reduction from 3-Coloring to positive 1-in-3-SAT.

Source instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...]}
Target instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[a, b, c], ...]}

Construction
------------
For every vertex v (0 <= v < n) and colour c in {1, 2, 3} introduce a Boolean
variable x(v, c), meaning "vertex v receives colour c".

  * Clause [x(v,1), x(v,2), x(v,3)] for every vertex v.  A 1-in-3 clause is
    satisfied exactly when one of its variables is true, so this forces each
    vertex to receive exactly one colour.

  * For every edge {u, v} and every colour c, introduce a fresh auxiliary
    variable y(u,v,c) and the clause [x(u,c), x(v,c), y(u,v,c)].  This clause
    is unsatisfiable iff both x(u,c) and x(v,c) are true; otherwise the
    auxiliary variable can be set to make it satisfied.  Hence it forbids the
    two endpoints of an edge from sharing colour c.  Each auxiliary occurs in
    exactly one clause, so distinct edge constraints never interfere.

The formula is satisfiable iff the graph has a proper 3-colouring.

Size: 3*n + 3*|E| variables and n + 3*|E| clauses, so the reduction runs in
polynomial time.
"""


def reduce(instance):
    n = instance["n"]
    edges = instance["edges"]

    # x(v, c) for v in 0..n-1, c in 1..3, numbered 1..3n.
    def x(v, c):
        return 3 * v + c

    clauses = []

    # Exactly one colour per vertex.
    for v in range(n):
        clauses.append([x(v, 1), x(v, 2), x(v, 3)])

    # Forbid equal colours on the endpoints of every edge.
    next_var = 3 * n
    for u, v in edges:
        for c in (1, 2, 3):
            next_var += 1
            y = next_var
            clauses.append([x(u, c), x(v, c), y])

    return {"num_vars": next_var, "clauses": clauses}
